question: Which layer does this module cover, and what question does it add to module 01?
options: Layer 2 (context): what the model sees on each call
Layer 1 (model): beyond choosing a model, whether to change its weights and whether to run it yourself
Layer 4 (loop): how work repeats until done
Layer 6 (governance): regulation only
explanation: Module 01 chose models as a buyer. This module stays in the model layer and looks inside: adapting weights, hosting open models and securing the artifacts.

question: Why are all lessons before the ADR quiz lessons, with no fine-tuning challenge?
options: Fine-tuning is no longer used in industry
The fake model can be fine-tuned only in Python
Training even a tiny model needs real compute, model downloads and a Python environment that a browser-only platform does not have yet; hands-on adaptation is planned for a later version
Adaptation decisions do not need evals
explanation: The module teaches the engineer's half of the job now (when to adapt, what it costs, how to review a plan). Hands-on training needs a separate architecture decision first.

question: A teammate proposes fine-tuning because answers "feel off". There is no eval set yet. What does this module say should happen first?
options: Fine-tune on all available data and compare by reading a few answers
Switch to the largest model available
Train a model from scratch
Build an eval set (module 10), measure the cheaper rungs (prompt, retrieval, examples), and climb only if they fail on cases that matter
explanation: Every decision in the module is gated by an eval. Without one, you cannot show that the lower rungs failed, nor that the fine-tuned model is better.

question: Which lesson answers "will this 8-billion-parameter model fit on our 24 GB GPU with 64 concurrent users?"
options: Lesson 07, local inference and quantization: weights plus KV cache memory math
Lesson 04, preference and reinforcement tuning
Lesson 05, synthetic data
Lesson 02, the adaptation ladder
explanation: Memory is parameters times bytes per weight, plus the KV cache that grows with context length and concurrency. Lesson 07 works through an example.

question: Why does the path include a lesson on the model supply chain?
options: Downloaded models cannot be fine-tuned
A model file is an artifact you load into your systems: some formats execute code on load, and you must know where it came from, under which license, and record it
Supply chains only matter for hardware
Open models are always malicious
explanation: Pickle-based checkpoints can run arbitrary code when loaded. Safetensors, pinned revisions, signatures and an AI-BOM make the artifact verifiable.

question: What does the ADR at the end of the module ask you to produce?
options: A fine-tuned model
A list of the most popular models on the Hub
An adaptation decision for a briefing: the rung, the data, the eval gate, the serving setup and the supply-chain checks, checked for coherence
A benchmark leaderboard
explanation: Like every module, it ends with a decision record. Tests check that the plan follows the briefing's eval results, memory limits, license and data rules.
